traveler: Edward Bulwer-Lytton, 1st Baron Lytton (Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer)
title: Baker Street to Knebworth: the Novelist, the Colonial Office, and the Word Vril
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: 31 Baker Street, London: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: At 31 Baker Street in Marylebone a son is born to General William Earle Bulwer of Heydon Hall and Elizabeth Barbara Lytton of Knebworth: one Norfolk family, one Hertfordshire family, neither yet certain which surname the child will carry. They christen him Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer. The street above the shops is quiet and Georgian and holds nothing of what is coming: no vril, no Rosicrucian rumour, no dark and stormy night. He is a younger son of the minor gentry, and the peerage is sixty-three years of work away.
suggested_refs: 31 Baker Street, Marylebone, the birthplace
sources: The Victorian Web, 'Edward Bulwer-Lytton: A Brief Biography'

stops.name: Heydon Hall, Norfolk: the general dies
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date (Victorian Web gives 7 July 1807); Heydon Hall as the place of death is the geography lens's assertion and is not independently corroborated
stops.campa: General William Earle Bulwer dies, and Edward is four. The hall stands behind its walled park in north Norfolk, Bulwer property for generations, and the boy is too young to inherit it or to register the loss. His mother takes her sons out of Norfolk soon after. Heydon becomes a name in the family's back-story rather than a place he returns to; the estate he will spend his life rebuilding is the other one, his mother's, thirty miles south at Knebworth.
suggested_refs: Heydon Hall, the Bulwer seat in north Norfolk

stops.name: St Lawrence, near Ramsgate: the grandfather's house
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the DNB gives the removal to Kent without a year
stops.campa: The widowed Elizabeth Bulwer settles her sons near her own father at St Lawrence, outside Ramsgate on the Kent coast. The boy grows up chiefly among women and books, precocious and sickly by his own later account, reading before he can properly write. The seaside town gives him none of the Gothic furniture his novels will be full of. No master supervises him for long, and what he knows he takes out of his grandfather's library. He is already certain that he is unlike other boys, and nobody in the house contradicts him.
suggested_refs: St Lawrence, near Ramsgate, the household of his maternal grandfather

stops.name: Fulham, Dr Ruddock's school: a fortnight
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by the Victorian Web; the DNB supplies the fortnight without a date
stops.campa: He is sent to Dr Ruddock's school at Fulham and taken away again within a fortnight, the first of several placements that fail. Fulham in these years is still a village of market gardens beyond the built edge of London, its school one of many small establishments drilling the sons of the gentry in Latin. Nothing of the visit survives except the fact and its brevity. A boy too clever or too unhappy for the regime is withdrawn almost as soon as he arrives, and his mother looks for another.
suggested_refs: Dr Ruddock's school at Fulham

stops.name: Rottingdean, Dr Hooker's school: the downs above the Channel
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the research pool carried '1812/1820', which cannot be both, and 1820 is excluded because the Victorian Web puts him at Ealing in summer 1820; Rottingdean falls between Fulham and Ealing, roughly 1815-1818
stops.campa: Dr Hooker keeps school at Rottingdean, on the chalk above the Channel, and here the boy stays longer than a fortnight. The village is a working fishing settlement, not yet a resort, the downs running bare to the cliff edge. He reads far outside the curriculum and begins writing verse in private, which his family, uncertain what to make of him, neither forbids nor encourages. Neither habit leaves him: he reads alone, and he writes where nobody is marking the result.
suggested_refs: Dr Hooker's school at Rottingdean, Sussex

stops.name: Ealing, the house of the Rev. Charles Wallington: Ismael
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Victorian Web places the tuition in summer 1820, correcting the pool's c.1818-1822
stops.campa: Ealing is a quiet Middlesex village west of London, and the Reverend Charles Wallington takes the seventeen-year-old through classics for Cambridge. The arrangement suits him as no institution ever has: one pupil, one tutor, a house rather than a dormitory. In the same year he publishes Ismael: An Oriental Tale, with Other Poems, juvenilia paid for and put into the world while he is still a schoolboy. He goes up to Cambridge already in print, before he has sat through a single lecture.
suggested_refs: Ismael: An Oriental Tale, with Other Poems (1820)

stops.name: Trinity College, Cambridge: the Easter term
stops.date_confidence: attested to the term (Easter 1822); the day is a placeholder
stops.campa: He enters Trinity in the Easter term, the grandest and most crowded college in Cambridge, and Great Court takes him as one more clever moneyed undergraduate among hundreds. He does not stay. Within a short time he moves to the smaller foundation nearer the river, and Trinity keeps him only long enough to matriculate. What Cambridge gives him is an audience outside his own family for the verse he has been writing since Rottingdean, and within three years a prize with the university's name on it.
suggested_refs: Great Court, Trinity College, Cambridge

stops.name: Ullswater: the grave remembered as Lucy
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the DNB relays his own account without a year
stops.campa: He travels north to the Lakes during the university years and visits, by his own account, the grave of an early love he remembers as Lucy. Ullswater lies long and narrow between the fells, already a pilgrimage for readers of Wordsworth, and the young Bulwer arrives as both mourner and tourist, folding a real grief into the fashionable melancholy of the district. He is twenty years old, has one book of verse in print, and has written no fiction at all. The account of the visit is his own, given years afterward, and nothing else records it.
suggested_refs: Ullswater and the Wordsworth pilgrimage country of the 1820s

stops.name: Trinity Hall, Cambridge: the Chancellor's Gold Medal
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: In July the university gives him the Chancellor's Gold Medal for English verse, for a poem called Sculpture. The prize is Cambridge's chief literary honour for undergraduates. The family that neither forbade nor encouraged the verse at Rottingdean now has the university's word for what he is. Trinity Hall is a small foundation in a narrow court by the river, older than Trinity and a fraction its size, and it suits him better than Great Court did.
suggested_refs: Sculpture, Chancellor's Gold Medal poem, Cambridge 1825

stops.name: Trinity Hall, Cambridge: the degree and Weeds and Wild Flowers
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: He takes the BA and prints, privately and at his own cost, a volume called Weeds and Wild Flowers. Private printing is the gentleman's way of publishing: no bookseller's risk, no reviewer's obligation, the edition given to friends. He also buys an army commission this year and will sell it in 1829 without ever having served. Two careers are bought and one is used. The poems go out to a few dozen people, the commission goes into a drawer, and the novels have not started yet.
suggested_refs: Weeds and Wild Flowers (1826), privately printed

segments.name: France, and a Marriage Against Advice

stops.name: Faubourg Saint-Germain, Paris: the salons
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1825-1826; the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: Fresh from the degree he crosses to Paris and moves through the salons of the Faubourg Saint-Germain, the old aristocratic quarter on the Left Bank still thick with returned emigres and Restoration politics. He is twenty-two and well connected, and the rooms he is let into discuss literature and government in the same breath. Cambridge has taught him nothing about rooms like these. Two years later he furnishes the drawing rooms of Pelham out of them.
suggested_refs: The Restoration salons of the Faubourg Saint-Germain

stops.name: Versailles, the park: the retreat from the salons
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1825-1826; the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: He withdraws from the salons to the woods around Versailles, where the old royal park stands half emptied of its Bourbon splendour and overgrown at the margins. The palace in these Restoration years is a monument to an absolutism restored on paper and not in fact. He reads and writes here at his own pace, an Englishman of twenty-three using the ruins of one nation's court as a private study, a morning's drive from the salon rooms he has stopped attending.
suggested_refs: The park and woods of Versailles under the Restoration

stops.name: Boulogne-sur-Mer: second in a duel
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the DNB gives the episode without date, principals, cause, or outcome
stops.campa: At Boulogne he acts as second in a duel. The record notes the fact and withholds the principals, the cause, and the outcome. The Channel port is thick with English residents living cheaply or avoiding creditors, an unofficial extension of English society planted on French sand, and quarrels that cannot be settled in London are sometimes carried across and settled here. He is a poet with a medal, a commission he will never use, and now a morning on a beach with pistols.
suggested_refs: The English colony at Boulogne-sur-Mer in the 1820s

stops.name: St James's Church, Piccadilly: the marriage to Rosina
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He marries Rosina Doyle Wheeler at St James's, Piccadilly, against his mother's strong objection to the match, and the objection has a price attached: the allowance stops. Wren's church stands at the centre of fashionable London and its register records a union both families expect little of. Today it is only a wedding, a young writer and an Irish beauty, neither yet famous. Within six years they will be separated, and within twelve she will publish a novel written to destroy him.
suggested_refs: St James's Church, Piccadilly, and its marriage register for 30 August 1827

stops.name: Woodcot, near Pangbourne: Falkland and Pelham
stops.date_confidence: attested for the novels; the Woodcot house itself is [R], the Victorian Web giving only 'Reading'
stops.campa: The couple keep house at Woodcot near Pangbourne, on the Thames west of Reading, and here the working novelist is made. Falkland appears in 1827 and does well in Germany and badly at home, where reviewers call it immoral. Pelham follows in 1828 and sells everything Falkland did not: a dandy's novel, worldly, ironic, instantly imitated. Their daughter Emily is born the same year. Nothing in the Berkshire countryside reaches the page. What the house holds is a career and a marriage, both of them starting in the same year and in the same rooms.
stops.quote: For though he is certainly a man who bathes and 'lives cleanly,' (two especial charges preferred against him by Messrs. the Great Unwashed,) yet he is also brave, generous, just; a true friend, an active citizen...
stops.quote_source: Paul Clifford (1830), Dedicatory Epistle of the first edition, on Pelham; Internet Archive scan paulclifford01lytt, footnote pp. xix-xx. Wiktionary cites this as the first published use of 'the great unwashed'. The epistle was dropped from later collected editions.
suggested_refs: Falkland (1827)
Pelham; or, The Adventures of a Gentleman (1828)

segments.name: Hertford Street, the Commons, the Bay of Naples

stops.name: Hertford Street, Mayfair: Paul Clifford opens in the rain
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the 36 Hertford Street address rests on History of Parliament Online, which returned HTTP 401 and could not be checked
stops.campa: The household moves into London, to Hertford Street in Mayfair, and the writing rate becomes industrial. He edits the New Monthly Magazine, publishes The Disowned and Devereux in a single year, and in 1830 puts out Paul Clifford, whose first sentence will outlive every other sentence he wrote, though not in the way he intended. He writes it as weather. A century and a half later it is a punchline, quoted by people who could not name the novel or the man.
stops.quote: It was a dark and stormy night; the rain fell in torrents, except at occasional intervals, when it was checked by a violent gust of wind which swept up the streets (for it is in London that our scene lies), rattling along the housetops, and fiercely agitating the scanty flame of the lamps that struggled against the darkness.
stops.quote_source: Paul Clifford (1830), opening sentence; verified verbatim against Project Gutenberg ebook 7735
suggested_refs: 36 Hertford Street, Mayfair
The New Monthly Magazine under his editorship

stops.name: St Ives, Cornwall: returned to Parliament
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: The borough of St Ives in Cornwall returns him to Parliament, and the novelist becomes a member at twenty-eight. He arrives in the Commons in the year of the Reform crisis, on the reforming side, and takes up causes a bestselling author is well placed to press: copyright for writers, an end to the Lord Chamberlain's monopoly over the theatres. His son Robert, who will govern India as viceroy and be buried in the family mausoleum, is born in November.
suggested_refs: The borough of St Ives before the Reform Act

stops.name: Lincoln: the seat held nine years
stops.date_confidence: attested: the seat runs 1832 to 1841
stops.campa: Reform gives him a safer and longer seat at Lincoln, which he holds for nine years, through Eugene Aram and The Last Days of Pompeii and the collapse of his marriage. The cathedral city on its steep hill is a long way from Hertfordshire and Mayfair, and the constituency's interests are nominally his while he goes on living and writing in London. He speaks for copyright reform and against theatrical censorship, and writes a novel most years he sits.
suggested_refs: The Lincoln constituency, 1832-1841

stops.name: Milan, Pinacoteca di Brera: the Briullov canvas
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: In Milan he sees Karl Briullov's enormous canvas of the last day of Pompeii, exhibited to crowds, and it gives him his book. The Russian's fleeing figures under a black sky, lit by falling fire, supply the central image before the Englishman has walked a single excavated street. The origin of the book is on record, and it is a painting in a northern Italian gallery, seen by an English tourist whose marriage is failing on the same journey. He has not yet been south.
suggested_refs: Karl Briullov, The Last Day of Pompeii, exhibited at Milan

stops.name: Naples: the bay under Vesuvius
stops.date_confidence: sources conflict on the Italian journey: one places it winter 1832-33, another autumn 1833 to spring 1834; neither is adopted here, and no source reached supports the tradition that the novel was written at Naples
stops.campa: Bulwer and Rosina come south to Naples, the bay under Vesuvius, on the Italian journey that finishes them as a couple. The mountain that buried the town he is about to write about stands over the city in plain view every morning. The quarrelling on this journey is public and it does not stop. Where the book was actually written is fixed by no source reached, and Naples is only where he stands. He is thirty, and after the journey home he will not live under the same roof as his wife again.
suggested_refs: The Bay of Naples and Vesuvius, 1833

stops.name: Pompeii, House of the Tragic Poet: cave canem
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no source fetched confirms that Bulwer entered the excavation at all
stops.campa: Tradition walks him through the excavated streets and into the House of the Tragic Poet, where the mosaic dog at the threshold barks its warning nineteen centuries after the ash. The house is said to be the model for the house of Glaucus in the novel. Whether Bulwer entered it is not recorded in anything reachable. The pilgrimage is made in his name by generations of English readers who came because of the book, guidebook in hand, looking for rooms he may never have seen.
suggested_refs: The House of the Tragic Poet, Pompeii, with its cave canem threshold mosaic
sources: Traditional account; not confirmed by Wikipedia, 'The Last Days of Pompeii'

stops.name: London: the separation from Rosina
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only; the pool's 'April' is corroborated by nothing reached
stops.campa: The separation from Rosina is made legal. She loses the children to him and begins a campaign that will run thirty years: pamphlets, letters posted to his constituents, a novel called Cheveley in 1839 written to expose him, and eventually a public denunciation at the hustings in front of the voters of Hertfordshire. He is a baronet by 1838 and a cabinet minister by 1858, and at every stage of the ascent his wife is in print somewhere, describing the man doing the climbing.
suggested_refs: Rosina Bulwer Lytton, Cheveley, or the Man of Honour (1839)

segments.name: The Name, the House, the Water Cure

stops.name: London, Covent Garden: Richelieu and the line that outran the play
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year and to Act II Scene II; the Covent Garden venue is reconstruction, not fixed by the verified pool
stops.campa: Richelieu; or, The Conspiracy reaches the London stage, and in the second act the old cardinal lifts a pen and speaks a line that will outlive the play and the author both, and go into common English with neither of them attached. He writes for the theatre in these years as deliberately as he writes novels, testing what an audience carries out of a building. He gets his answer twice in one lifetime, and both times for a sentence he did not think was the point.
stops.quote: True, — THIS! / Beneath the rule of men entirely great / The pen is mightier than the sword. Behold / The arch-enchanter's wand! — itself a nothing! — / But taking sorcery from the master-hand / To paralyse the Caesars — and to strike / The loud earth breathless! — Take away the sword — / States can be saved without it!
stops.quote_source: Richelieu; or, The Conspiracy (1839), Act II Scene II, first edition; Internet Archive scan richelieuorconsp00lyttuoft. The popular short form conflates two passages four lines apart without an ellipsis.
suggested_refs: Richelieu; or, The Conspiracy (1839), first edition

stops.name: Theatre Royal, Haymarket: Money
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Money opens at the Theatre Royal, Haymarket, a comedy about inheritance, courtship, and what a legacy does to the people standing nearest it. It is his most durable play, revived for a century after the novels have stopped being read, and it is written by a man whose own inheritance is three years off and whose own courtship ended in a legal separation. The Haymarket audience laughs at the sudden fortune of Alfred Evelyn. Their author is waiting for one.
suggested_refs: Money (1840), Theatre Royal Haymarket

stops.name: London: Zanoni
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: Zanoni appears: an immortal Rosicrucian adept, a novice who fails at the threshold, the Dweller on the Threshold itself, and the guillotine waiting at the end of the Terror. He has written a novel in which occult knowledge is real, costly, and fatal to the unprepared, and readers who want it to be a coded manual rather than a story begin, from this book onward, to treat him as an initiate writing under cover. He never says he is one. He never quite says he is not.
stops.quote: Man is arrogant in proportion to his ignorance.
stops.quote_source: Zanoni (1842), Book IV; attributed via Wikiquote and NOT verified against a primary edition [R]
suggested_refs: Zanoni (1842)

stops.name: Knebworth House: the mother's will and the royal licence
stops.date_confidence: attested: mother dies December 1843, royal licence 20 February 1844
stops.campa: His mother dies in December and Knebworth comes to him with a condition in the will: he must take the Lytton name. By royal licence in February he becomes Edward Bulwer-Lytton and assumes the Lytton arms. Then he rebuilds the house, turning a plain Georgian front into the turreted Tudor-Gothic pile that still stands, gargoyles and all, and leaves an instruction above his mother's mantelpiece that her room be kept as she left it. The baronetcy, the peerage, and vril all proceed from this address.
suggested_refs: Knebworth House, rebuilt 1843-1845
The royal licence of 20 February 1844

stops.name: Weimar: the Schiller translations
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction of both date and place: the DNB names 'Germany' and no town, and the pool's 1841-1843 dating rested on a false causal link to a separation of 1833 and 1836; the translations appear in the mid-1840s
stops.campa: He spends a period in Germany learning the language and translating Friedrich Schiller, whose ballads and dramas shape the verse he writes afterward. No source names the town. Weimar stands here for a residence the record leaves general: the small ducal capital that holds Schiller's memory more closely than anywhere else, and the obvious destination for an Englishman studying him. The pin marks where the reading was done, not a house anyone can point to.
suggested_refs: Bulwer-Lytton's translations of Schiller, mid-1840s

stops.name: Great Malvern: the cold-water cure
stops.date_confidence: the Victorian Web gives no date at all for the water cures beyond mid-century; the sequence 1845-1847 is spacing, not testimony
stops.campa: Chronic ill health sends him to the water cure at Malvern, nine or ten weeks of cold baths, wet sheets, and controlled diet under the hydropathic regime the Victorian invalid class swears by. He follows it later under a Doctor Weiss at Petersham on the Thames, seven weeks more. A novelist whose books are full of mesmerists and adepts submits himself to the era's own half-medical enthusiasm, and goes back for more of it. The Victorian Web gives no date for any of the cures.
stops.quote: What men want is not talent, it is purpose,—in other words, not the power to achieve, but the will to labour.
stops.quote_source: Lucretia; or, The Children of Night (1846), Part II; attributed via secondary compilation and NOT verified against a primary edition [R]
suggested_refs: The Malvern hydropathic establishments
Petersham on the Thames, under Doctor Weiss

stops.name: Boppard on the Rhine: Doctor Schmidt
stops.date_confidence: undated in the Victorian Web; the year is spacing, not testimony
stops.campa: The cure continues at Boppard on the Rhine, under a Doctor Schmidt, in an old Roman town on a bend of the river already established as a resort for European invalids. Three countries and three doctors have now had the same patient. The underlying complaint, a diseased middle ear that will eventually kill him, is untouched by any of it. He goes back to Hertfordshire, to the novels and the party managers, with the ear no better and the regime faithfully kept.
suggested_refs: The hydropathic establishment at Boppard am Rhein

stops.name: Houses of Parliament, Westminster: member for Hertfordshire
stops.date_confidence: attested: the seat runs 1852 to 1866
stops.campa: Returned as Conservative member for Hertfordshire, he takes his seat in the new Palace of Westminster and holds it fourteen years. The Caxtons in 1849 had already restored him as a novelist after the bad decade, a domestic family chronicle from the man who wrote Rosicrucian adepts. Now the second career runs beside the first, novel and division list, and neither one gives way to the other. From 1858 he adds a cabinet department to the arrangement.
stops.quote: Master books, but do not let them master you. Read to live, not live to read.
stops.quote_source: The Caxtons: A Family Picture (1849), Part II; attributed via secondary compilation and NOT verified against a primary edition [R]
suggested_refs: The Caxtons: A Family Picture (1849)

stops.name: Knebworth Park: the Guild of Literature and Art
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1854 incorporation; the exact acreage of the gift is not fixed by any source reached
stops.campa: He gives land beside the Knebworth estate to the Guild of Literature and Art, the scheme he founds with Charles Dickens to build almshouses for writers and artists who end their lives poor. The Guild is incorporated in 1854; Dickens acts in the amateur theatricals that raise its money, and Bulwer-Lytton supplies the acres. A landed baronet uses his own park to underwrite the trade he made his fortune in. The Guild is wound up by Act of Parliament in 1897, its houses never much occupied.
suggested_refs: The Guild of Literature and Art, incorporated 1854, dissolved 1897

stops.name: Glasgow: Rector of the University
stops.date_confidence: attested: Wikipedia gives the rectorship as 1856-1859, correcting the pool's single year
stops.campa: The students of Glasgow elect him Rector, and he holds the office three years. The post is honorific and its duty is an address: a novelist, playwright, and member of Parliament stands before a Scottish university and tells young men what a working life of the mind requires. He is fifty-three years old. The Colonial Office is two years off and The Coming Race is fifteen, and nobody in the hall, the speaker included, can tell which of the two the name will end up attached to.
stops.quote: Even genius itself is but fine observation strengthened by fixity of purpose.
stops.quote_source: Caxtoniana: A Series of Essays on Life, Literature, and Manners (1863), Essay VII; attributed via Wikiquote and NOT verified against a primary edition [R]
suggested_refs: The Rectorship of the University of Glasgow, 1856-1859

stops.name: Colonial Office, Downing Street: Secretary of State
stops.date_confidence: attested: 5 June 1858 to 11 June 1859, correcting the pool's garbled phrasing
stops.campa: He is Secretary of State for the Colonies in Derby's government for one year and six days, working from the Colonial Office in Downing Street. From this desk he selects Richard Clement Moody to take the Royal Engineers to the Fraser River and found the colony of British Columbia. Empire is administered here on paper, at four months' distance by sailing packet, by a man who will never cross the Atlantic to see a single acre of what he is disposing of.
stops.quote: No happiness without order, no order without authority, no authority without unity.
stops.quote_source: The Coming Race (1871), Chapter IX, given by the narrator as an admittedly lossy paraphrase of a Vril-ya proverb; Project Gutenberg ebook 1951
suggested_refs: The Colonial Office, Downing Street
Richard Clement Moody and the Columbia Detachment

stops.name: Lytton, British Columbia: Fort Dallas renamed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1858; the month is a placeholder set after his June appointment
stops.campa: At the confluence the Nlaka'pamux call Camchin, where the Thompson runs into the Fraser, Governor James Douglas renames the post of Fort Dallas after his Colonial Secretary. Lytton, British Columbia, takes the name of a Hertfordshire novelist who has never been within five thousand miles of it and never will be. The gold rush is working the bars below the town. His name sits on the map of a country he governs by dispatch and knows from other men's reports.
suggested_refs: Lytton, British Columbia, at the Thompson-Fraser confluence

stops.name: London: A Strange Story
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: A Strange Story appears: an elixir of life, a mesmerist villain, a rationalist physician forced to concede that the world holds more than his instruments record. Three years earlier he had published The Haunted and the Haunters, a London house with a room no one survives in, still anthologised as one of the best ghost stories in the language. The cabinet minister of 1858 is writing about immortality by chemistry, and his readers are no longer sure which of the two is the disguise.
suggested_refs: A Strange Story (1862)
The Haunted and the Haunters; or, The House and the Brain (1859)

stops.name: Palace of Westminster: Baron Lytton of Knebworth
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: He is created Baron Lytton of Knebworth and crosses from the Commons to the Lords, ending thirty-five years on and off the green benches. A younger son with no estate, living in 1827 on an allowance his mother stopped, now sits in the Lords under a title of his own making. His wife, who has spent three decades telling the public what kind of man is doing the climbing, is still alive and still writing. His son Robert will be Viceroy of India within ten years.
suggested_refs: The barony of Lytton of Knebworth, created 1866

stops.name: Aldermanbury, London: the Rosicrucian claim
stops.date_confidence: attested for the SRIA's founding at Aldermanbury on 1 June 1867; Bulwer-Lytton's connection to it is [R] and unconfirmed
stops.campa: The Societas Rosicruciana in Anglia is formally established at Aldermanbury by Robert Wentworth Little, and the occult revival it belongs to will later claim Bulwer-Lytton as patron, honorary Grand Patron, or secret adept, depending on who is telling it. The society's own account of its founding does not mention him. He is alive, famous, and four years from writing the book that will make the claim irresistible, and nobody in this room appears to have asked him.
stops.quote: It can destroy like the flash of lightning; yet, differently applied, it can replenish or invigorate life, heal, and preserve...
stops.quote_source: The Coming Race (1871), Chapter IX, on vril; Project Gutenberg ebook 1951. Quoted mid-sentence at both ends, hence the ellipsis.
suggested_refs: The Societas Rosicruciana in Anglia, established 1 June 1867
sources: Wikipedia, 'Societas Rosicruciana in Anglia' (which does not mention Bulwer-Lytton)

stops.name: St James's Palace: Knight Grand Cross
stops.date_confidence: sources conflict: Wikipedia gives 18 January 1870, the Victorian Web gives 15 January; the 18th is used here and the disagreement is not resolved
stops.campa: He is made Knight Grand Cross of the Order of St Michael and St George, the order that decorates service to the colonies, eleven years after the year he spent running them. He is sixty-six and four years in the Lords, and this is the last thing the Crown gives him. Wikipedia dates it the eighteenth of January and the Victorian Web the fifteenth; the disagreement stands unresolved. He dies on the eighteenth of January, three years from now, and there is one book left that anyone will remember.
suggested_refs: The Order of St Michael and St George, Knight Grand Cross, January 1870
sources: The Victorian Web, 'A Brief Biography' (giving 15 January)

stops.name: Knebworth House, the study: Vril
stops.date_confidence: attested; canonical atlas pin inherited from maria_orsic.journey.json
stops.campa: In the study at Knebworth he writes The Coming Race, and Blackwood publishes it anonymously in May: a mining engineer falls into a subterranean world of winged, calm, immensely powerful people who have mastered a single force that does everything. He calls the force vril. To his friend John Forster he explains that he means electricity developed to uses only dimly guessed at, not mesmerism. The word leaves the book almost at once and never comes back, and a beef extract and a German myth are both waiting for it.
stops.quote: I should call it electricity, except that it comprehends in its manifold branches other forces of nature, to which, in our scientific nomenclature, differing names are assigned, such as magnetism, galvanism, &c.
stops.quote_source: The Coming Race (1871), Chapter VII, the vril definition; verified verbatim against Project Gutenberg ebook 1951

stops.name: Torquay, Argyll Hall: the last months
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He spends his last months at Torquay on the Devon coast, at Argyll Hall, with his son Robert's family, taking the mild sea air that Victorian medicine still prescribes for the chronically ill. The middle-ear disease he has carried for decades has gone into the brain. He dies at about two in the morning on the eighteenth of January, sixty-nine years old, three years to the day after the Grand Cross. Kenelm Chillingly and The Parisians are published in the year of his death.

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, St Edmund's Chapel: buried against his wishes
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Dean refuses him the Abbey. John Forster argues that if a writer of this standing is kept out then no writer can be let in; a letter appears in The Times; the Dean relents. He is buried on the twenty-fifth of January, not in Poets' Corner but in St Edmund's Chapel, under a black marble slab cut with two dates, near the tomb of Sir Humphrey Bourchier, who died at Barnet and turns up as a character in one of his own historical romances. He had wanted Knebworth.

stops.name: 17 Lansdowne Road, London: Blavatsky and The Secret Doctrine
stops.date_confidence: attested; pin and date inherited from blavatsky.journey.json
stops.campa: At 17 Lansdowne Road in Holland Park, Helena Blavatsky finishes The Secret Doctrine, seventeen years after The Coming Race and a few miles from the rooms where London first argued about it. Vril passes into Theosophy as a fact of nature rather than a device of fiction, and from Theosophy it goes everywhere. Blavatsky's own atlas file never names Bulwer-Lytton. The word travels without him. Readers who never open the novel treat his invention as a disclosure.

stops.name: Munich: the Vril Gesellschaft takes the word
stops.date_confidence: traditional; pin and date inherited from maria_orsic.journey.json, whose own confidence field reads 'traditional'
stops.campa: In Munich, Maria Orsic and the woman remembered as Traute give their circle a name taken from an English novel: the Vril Gesellschaft. Forty-eight years after a Hertfordshire baron sat in his study and coined a word for a force that heals and destroys, German women are using it as an emblem for a society whose membership no archive holds. The word arrives in Bavaria intact. Everything else about the society is contested, and the earliest hard trace of it is a recollection written down in 1947.
stops.quote: The fire lodged in the hollow of a rod directed by the hand of a child could shatter the strongest fortress, or cleave its burning way from the van to the rear of an embattled host.

stops.name: Knebworth Park, the Lytton Mausoleum: the granddaughter's ashes
stops.date_confidence: attested for the interment of Constance Bulwer-Lytton in the year of her death, 1923; the day is a placeholder
stops.campa: The octagonal mausoleum John Buonarotti Papworth built in Knebworth Park in 1817, commissioned by Edward's mother for her own parents and holding her since 1843, receives the ashes of his granddaughter Constance Bulwer-Lytton: suffragette, hunger striker, force-fed in Walton Gaol under the false name Jane Warton after they had refused to do it to a peer's daughter. His son Robert lies here too, brought back from the viceroyalty of India. The founder of the line is in Westminster, alone.

stops.name: San Jose State University: the contest in his name
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of founding; the contest ran to January 2025
stops.campa: At San Jose State University, Professor Scott Rice founds a contest inviting the world to submit the worst possible opening sentence to a novel that does not exist, and names it after Edward Bulwer-Lytton. Entries arrive by the thousand every year for forty-three seasons, until Rice ends it in January 2025, citing his age. The man was a baron, a cabinet minister, and the author of The Last Days of Pompeii. He is now a category of bad weather in a first line.
